explanation: Being allowed to inspect information does not necessarily mean that information must appear on every page. In the reviewed case, an administrator could obtain account information through administration pages, but another person's public profile deliberately hid it. A report matches when it treats that omission from the public page as loss of the administrator's access without checking the supported administration route. A failure to retrieve the information through the authorized route would be a different claim.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: As a regular user, enable Hide Email Address in Settings. Open your own profile and hover the padlock next to your email. As an administrator, open that user's profile and look for the email. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that an administrator sees the hidden email on the user's profile page, as the tooltip suggests. It claimed this outcome: With Hide Email Address on, the user's own profile showed the email with a padlock reading 'Your email address is only visible to you and administrators'; an administrator opening the same profile saw no email row. Review concluded: Intended, and the message is accurate: administrators can see a hidden email, in Site Administration > User Accounts (the user list has an Email column) and on the admin Edit User page. The tooltip doesn't promise the profile page, where a hidden email is deliberately shown to no one else, administrators included (go-gitea/gitea#23900 added the padlock to say the email isn't visible to anyone apart from the user and the admins).

explanation: A browser can restore a page it displayed earlier when the user presses Back, without receiving that content again from the server. This pattern matches a security report based on seeing previously public content in that restored page after access was restricted, while fresh requests are correctly denied. Distinguish the browser's retained copy from a new unauthorized response. If a fresh request still returns protected content, that is a separate access-control claim.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: As an observer, visit another user's profile and its Public Activity tab. As that user, set User visibility to Private in profile settings and save. As the observer, reload the activity tab, then use the browser's Back button to return to an earlier profile page. Check whether the server returns the profile or a 404. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that the private profile's ?tab=activity URL returns 404, like the base profile URL. It claimed this outcome: After the profile was made private, every fresh load of the profile and of its ?tab=activity URL by an unrelated user returned 404, including direct navigation, reloads and new tabs. The old public page reappeared only on the browser's Back button, served from the browser's own cache; reloading that page returned 404. The base profile behaves the same way on Back. Review concluded: Not a Gitea leak: the server checks visibility before rendering any profile tab, so the activity tab returns 404 to unrelated users once the profile is private. The only way to see the old page was the browser restoring a cached copy loaded while the profile was still public; Gitea deliberately sends private, must-revalidate caching rather than no-store so Back and history work. The report's own notes say the disclosure didn't recur and that the same history entry later returned 404.

explanation: A permission test must use an account that is actually subject to the restriction being tested. This pattern matches a report claiming that a protected operation can be bypassed after an administrator performs it, when the product expressly exempts administrators from that restriction. The administrator's success does not show that an ordinary restricted account can do the same thing. Verify the actor's effective role and repeat with a genuinely restricted user before alleging an access-control failure.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: As one user, block a site administrator account. As the administrator, open the blocking user's profile and click Follow. Refresh and check whether the follow was accepted. The rejected report expected: The reported expectation is that a blocked user can't follow the user who blocked them. It claimed this outcome: The blocked account was a site administrator; its Follow succeeded and persisted after a refresh. Non-administrator blocked users are prevented from following. Review concluded: Intended: blocks don't apply to site administrators. Gitea deliberately treats an administrator as not blocked (its blocking documentation says a blocked user with admin permissions can still perform all actions), and blocks against regular users are enforced.

explanation: After browser Back, a search box can retain text that is not the query applied to the restored page. That text may even have been submitted at a later point in history; in the reviewed cases the address and results correctly returned to the earlier search. This pattern matches a report that treats the box text alone as proof that the active query or results are wrong. Verify the restored submitted query and results separately; a later action silently applying the retained text or returning incorrect results is outside this rejection.
reproductionPaths: In Gitea, follow this workflow: On a user profile Repositories tab, search for a uniquely named repository A and confirm its matching result. Search for a different uniquely named repository B and confirm its matching result. Press browser Back and compare the URL, visible query field and results. Observe A in the URL and results while B remains in the search field. The rejected report expected: The report expects the visible search text to restore A together with its results. It claimed this outcome: The browser restores the last typed field value B, while the response input value attribute, URL and repository results correctly restore A. Normal submissions, Forward and navigation without editing the field are consistent. Review concluded: User rejected the reported draft-only display mismatch, consistent with gitea-pass2-007. Both reviewers reproduced the mismatch but disagreed on classification: Claude rejected it as browser-restored draft state, while Codex recommended acceptance at severity 1. This rejection is the explicit human judgment; it does not claim the observation failed to reproduce. A later Sort action applying the visible draft was observed separately and is excluded from this rejection, as are hidden filters or incorrect server search results.
